segments.original: Hollywood musicals are deeply associated with the golden age of American cinema, but they did not disappear with the end of the studio system. Instead, they changed shape. The traditional musical could still be found often, slightly reworked to suit a more modern audience.

segments.original: Brian (Michael York) arrives in Berlin in 1931. He meets Sally Bowles (Liza Minnelli) and the two become lovers. She works at the Kit Kat Klub (note the three Ks), an underground cabaret cut off from the outside world. segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Glimpses of Nazi brutality go unnoticed by those enjoying themselves at the cabaret. The songs bring the plot and characters to life, driving the narrative while also commenting on the unfolding events. "Maybe This Time" expresses Sally's high hopes; "If You Could See Her" is a terrifying allegory of the intense persecution of Berlin's Jewish population. The songs are performed on the stage of the Kit Kat Klub and, apart from the expressionist angles revealing morally gray spectators, the numbers are staged realistically. Fosse shows the performances from a distance, using the glare of the lights to emphasize the small stage and the silhouettes of heads in the audience - conspirators in this dark world.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Bob Fosse (1927-1989) was the dominant force in the American musical from the late 1960s onward. A choreographer by training, Fosse created a singular style that used every limb to accentuate a dancer's movement. His Cabaret (1972) won eight Oscars, while All That Jazz (1979), a frank, semi-autobiographical account of a director on the verge of collapse amid preparations for his next show, was awarded the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

segments.original: Rock dominated most musicals from the 1970s onward. Alan Parker (b. 1944), who also directed Bugsy Malone (1976) and Fame (1980), directed Pink Floyd: The Wall (1982). segments.original: Richard O'Brien's offbeat stage musical, adapted for the screen in 1975, was a flop on its release. However, when a New York theater began showing it at midnight screenings, word quickly spread about the bizarre science fiction and horror spoof. The film became a cult hit and to this day holds the record for the longest theatrical run, having been shown at the same theater in Munich, Germany, every week for more than 27 years.

segments.original: A very young Susan Sarandon (b. 1946) and Barry Bostwick (b. 1945) star as Janet and Brad, an innocent couple whose car breaks down on a stormy night, forcing them to seek shelter in a nearby castle, unaware that it belongs to the stockings-and-garters-clad transvestite Frank N. Furter (Tim Curry, reprising his stage role) and his friends from Transylvania, including the sinister Riff Raff (Richard O'Brien) and Magenta (Patricia Quinn). Also living in the mansion are the biker Eddie (Meat Loaf), a failed creation (in the style of Frankenstein's monster) of Frank N. Furter, and Rocky (Peter Hinwood), his perfectly tanned replacement/upgrade.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Narrated by Dr. Everett Scott (Jonathan Adams) and driven by glam rock, the film is a celebration of sexuality: Frank N. Furter and his troupe try to seduce the virginal Brad and Janet to the tune of memorable songs such as "Touch-a Touch-a Touch Me", "Sweet Transvestite" and, of course, "Time Warp". The mix of brazen sexuality, ironic quips, outrageous costumes, and double entendres is unlike anything ever done in cinema. It is easy to see why the catchy songs and highly quotable dialogue became such a huge hit with fans, the most enthusiastic of whom dress up as the characters, act out parts of the film during screenings, and bring props to use at specific moments in the film, for example, throwing rice during the wedding scene. The Rocky Horror Picture Show may not be a film for the whole family, but it is still fantastic kitsch fun.
